title: Invertebrates
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 6 Science and Technology; not yet checked by a CBC Science and Technology teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: A nature walk with jars and a hand lens: ants, a spider in a web (looked at, not touched), an earthworm after rain, a snail, a millipede. Counting legs and body parts on the real animal, then putting it back where it was found.

skills.key_step: The child names the common groups of invertebrates (insects, spiders, millipedes and centipedes, crustaceans, worms, snails and slugs) with a Kenyan example of each.

floor.prerequisite: Can sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates.
floor.question: Does an ant have a backbone?

representations: animals seen on a nature walk
a table of groups and examples
steps: Insects: six legs, three parts (ant, bee, butterfly).
Soft bodies: earthworm, snail, slug; hard shell in water: crab.
contexts: a market stall with crabs at the coast

board.do: Draw an ant, a spider and a millipede.

board.say: How many legs? Is it an insect?

board.do: Wait for the child to count and decide.
Write the group under each animal.

misconceptions.ask: How many legs does a spider have?
misconceptions.repair: Spiders have eight legs; insects have six.

listen_for: a worm is not an animal group
misconceptions.ask: Does an earthworm have a backbone? Is it an animal?
misconceptions.repair: Worms and snails are invertebrate groups.

misconceptions.ask: Does a crab have fins and gills like a tilapia?
How many legs did you count?
misconceptions.repair: Insects have six legs; a millipede has many.

checks.question: Give an example of an insect and of a spider.
checks.answer: for example an ant and a house spider

checks.question: To which group does an earthworm belong?

skills.key_step: The child describes the general features of invertebrates (no backbone, many with a hard outer cover or a soft body) and of each group (insects: six jointed legs, three body parts, many with wings; spiders: eight legs, two parts).
representations: a hand lens on an ant and a spider
a table of features by group
steps: Insects: three body parts, six legs, often wings and feelers.
Spiders: two parts, eight legs, no feelers or wings.
Worms: soft, no legs; snails: soft with a shell outside.
contexts: a snail on the school wall

board.do: Draw an insect with three body parts.
Ask the child to draw a spider's two parts.

listen_for: all of them have six legs
misconceptions.repair: Insects six, spiders eight, millipedes many.

misconceptions.ask: How big can an octopus or a giant snail grow?

misconceptions.repair: Worms and snails have no legs.

misconceptions.ask: Is the shell inside or outside the body?
misconceptions.repair: A shell is outside; there is no backbone.

checks.question: How many body parts and legs does an insect have?
checks.answer: three body parts and six legs

checks.question: Give one feature all invertebrates share.

skills.key_step: The child outlines helpful invertebrates (bees pollinate and give honey, earthworms mix and air the soil, silkworms give silk) and harmful ones (mosquitoes spread malaria, houseflies spread cholera, ticks, crop pests), matching each to its effect.

floor.question: To which group does a mosquito belong?

representations: a chart: invertebrate, helpful or harmful, how
pictures of a beehive and a mosquito net
steps: Match pests to the disease or damage.

board.do: Draw a mosquito, a housefly and an earthworm.
Ask the child to write helpful or harmful under each.

misconceptions.ask: What do bees and earthworms do for farmers?
Which insect bites at night and spreads malaria?
misconceptions.repair: Mosquitoes spread malaria; houseflies spread cholera and typhoid germs.

misconceptions.ask: What does soil with earthworms look like?
misconceptions.repair: Earthworms mix and air the soil.

misconceptions.ask: What do bees carry between flowers?

checks.question: Give one helpful and one harmful invertebrate.
How do earthworms help a farmer?
checks.answer: they mix and air the soil and help dead matter rot

skills.key_step: The child chooses safe and kind ways of handling invertebrates: look with a hand lens, use a jar or gloves, never touch stinging or biting ones, wash hands after, keep them only a short time and return them.

floor.prerequisite: Knows some invertebrates sting or bite.
floor.question: Name one invertebrate that stings.

representations: a jar with air holes, gloves and a hand lens
a picture of a safari ant line
steps: Look first; do not touch unknown animals.
Use a jar with air holes or gloves.
Study for a short time, then return it.
contexts: a nature walk in the school compound
a hairy caterpillar on a tree

board.do: Draw a jar with a lid.

board.say: What does a grasshopper in here need?

board.do: Ask the child to add air holes and a leaf.

listen_for: pick it up with your hand
misconceptions.ask: What can a hairy caterpillar do to your skin?
misconceptions.repair: Use a jar or gloves; some sting or bite.

listen_for: it does not matter if it dies
misconceptions.ask: Is it still living? Can we study it alive?
misconceptions.repair: Handle small animals gently and return them.

misconceptions.ask: What could be on the soil and the animal?
misconceptions.repair: Wash hands with soap after handling.

misconceptions.ask: What does the grasshopper need to live?
misconceptions.repair: Give air and food, and return it soon.

checks.question: Give one safe way to look at a spider.
checks.answer: look with a hand lens without touching, or use a jar

checks.question: What should you do after handling earthworms?
checks.answer: wash your hands with soap and return the worms to the soil
